findings.title: A shortened route with a distant end
findings.claim: The immediate can be pictured as a shortened route: initial quickening reduces the distance to acquisition, while the later fire contact and expulsion reverse that nearness by making the end a place of exclusion.
findings.mechanism: The focus's immediate-horizon noun and accelerated-giving verb carry nearness and speed. The supplied contrast between preferring worldly life and what is better and more enduring in 87:16-17 makes the route facet an apt analogy. In 79:38-39, preference for worldly life is followed by fire as an abode; in 7:18, an exit command is paired with the expelled status and Jahannam. Together these contacts turn quick acquisition into a path whose ending is far from acceptance.
findings.reader_payoff: The speed of arrival and the distance of the final outcome become part of one trajectory: what is near to acquire can end in exclusion from proximity.
findings.containment: The focus names an immediate horizon and accelerated giving, not a literal journey. The registry limits the shortcut sense to travel and roads, so it is retained by analogy. The 7:18 parallel supplies an expulsion pattern, not a claim that its following collective is the focus's subject; no single outcome is asserted for every worldly desire.

epistemic.reason: The support is trusted but carries its own weak grade. Exact connection Arabic grounds the endpoint parallels, while the road-to-temporal-horizon transfer remains analogical.

findings.title: Desire within an apportioned grant
findings.claim: Desire for the immediate sets a direction but does not command the scope or final result of the grant: wider parallels describe both a limited share and complete recompense within present life, while provision remains subject to expansion and restriction and the focus ends in expulsion.
findings.mechanism: The focus carrier is the desire to reach the immediate; its accelerated grant is expressly framed by what is willed and for whom. In 42:20 a worldly aim receives some of its harvest and no later share, while 11:15 describes full recompense for deeds within worldly life. The 17:30 provision statement adds expansion and restriction by will, and 7:18 supplies an exit-and-expulsion pattern. These contacts make the doubled haste a speed of allocation, not evidence that desire controls amount or destination.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can distinguish how quickly something is given, how much belongs to a chosen horizon, and where the same person's course ends.
findings.containment: The full-present recompense in 11:15 and the limited share in 42:20 remain separate formulations; neither is used to select a single rule for 17:18. The unresolved sh-y branch mappings are excluded, and the focus's wording about what and whom is willed is retained only at surface level.

epistemic.reason: The source walk is legacy-unbound, while the cited connections supply exact Arabic and distinct allocation frames. Their parallels support a bounded reading without settling how the focus's clauses are scoped.
